title: Of the most excellent men
paragraphs: If I were asked which men, of all I have come across, I would pick, I should answer that, to my mind, I find three I rank above the rest.

One is Homer. Not that Aristotle or Varro, for example, were not perhaps as learned as he was; nor that Virgil was not his equal in his own art — that I leave to those who know them both to settle. I, who only really understand one of them, can only say this, by my poor lights: that I do not believe the Muses themselves could ever go beyond the Roman:
"Tale facit carmen docta testudine, quale Cynthius impositis temperat articulis:"
["He plays on his learned lyre a verse such as Cynthian Apollo modulates with his imposed fingers." — Propertius, ii. 34, 79.]

and yet, when we say this, we must not forget that it is mainly from Homer that Virgil draws his excellence — that Homer is his guide and teacher, and that one stroke of the Iliad gave him the body and matter from which to put together his great and divine Aeneid. But that is not all I am reckoning with: I add several other circumstances that make this poet seem to me admirable, almost beyond human condition. And, in truth, I often wonder that the man who produced — and gave their place in the world to — so many gods was not made a god himself. Blind and poor, living before the sciences had been put into rule and definite observation, he knew them so well that all who have since undertaken to set up governments, to wage wars, or to write either about religion or about philosophy, of whatever sect, or about the arts, have used him as the most perfect instructor in every kind of knowledge, and his books as a treasury of every sort of learning:
"Qui, quid sit pulcrum, quid turpe, quid utile, quid non, Planius ac melius Chrysippo et Crantore dicit:"
["Who tells us what is fair, what foul, what useful, what not, more clearly and better than Chrysippus and Crantor?" — Horace, Epistles, i. 2, 3.]
and, as another says,
"A quo, ceu fonte perenni, Vatum Pieriis ora rigantur aquis"
["From whom, as from a perennial spring, the lips of poets are moistened with Pierian waters." — Ovid, Amores, iii. 9, 25.]
and another,
"Adde Heliconiadum comites, quorum unus Homerus Sceptra potitus;"
["Add the companions of the Muses, of whom Homer alone has won the sceptre." — Lucretius, iii. 1050.]
and another:
"Cujusque ex ore profusos Omnis posteritas latices in carmina duxit, Amnemque in tenues ausa est deducere rivos. Unius foecunda bonis."

["From whose mouth all posterity has drawn copious streams of verse, and has dared to channel the mighty river into its little rivulets, fertile in the wealth of one man." — Manilius, Astronomica, ii. 8.]

It is against the order of nature that he should have made the most excellent thing that can be made; for the ordinary birth of things is imperfect — they grow and gather strength by growing — whereas he made the infancy of poetry and of several other sciences mature, perfect, and complete at the outset. For that reason he can be called the first and last of poets, in keeping with the fine testimony antiquity has left of him: "as there was no one before him whom he could imitate, so there has been no one since who could imitate him." His words, according to Aristotle, are the only words that have motion and action, the only substantial words. Alexander the Great, having found a rich casket among Darius' spoils, ordered it be set aside to keep his Homer in, saying that Homer was the best and most faithful counsellor he had in his military affairs. For the same reason Cleomenes, son of Anaxandridas, said that Homer was the poet of the Spartans, as being an excellent master of the discipline of war. There is also this singular tribute to him in Plutarch's judgment: that he is the only author in the world who never glutted or sickened his readers, always presenting himself as something new, and always flourishing in some fresh grace. That naughty Alcibiades, asking one who pretended to learning for a book of Homer, gave him a box on the ear because he had none — which he thought as scandalous as we should if we found one of our priests without a breviary. Xenophanes complained one day to Hiero, tyrant of Syracuse, that he was so poor he could not afford to keep two servants. "What!" Hiero replied. "Homer, who was much poorer than you, keeps more than ten thousand, though he is dead." What did Panaetius leave unsaid when he called Plato the Homer of the philosophers? Besides, what glory can be compared to his? Nothing is more constantly on men's lips than his name and works; nothing is so well known and accepted as Troy, Helen, and the war fought over her — when perhaps there never was such a thing. Our children are still called by names he invented more than three thousand years ago; who does not know Hector and Achilles? Not only certain particular families but most nations also trace their origins to his inventions. Mehmed II, emperor of the Turks, writing to our Pope Pius II, said, "I am astonished the Italians take up arms against me, considering we share a common descent from the Trojans, and it is just as much my business as theirs to revenge the blood of Hector on the Greeks, whom they side with against me." Is it not a noble farce, in which kings, republics, and emperors have played their parts for so many ages, with the vast universe for a stage? Seven Greek cities contended for the honour of being his birthplace — so much honour even his obscurity helped him to:
"Smyrna, Rhodos, Colophon, Salamis, Chios, Argos, Athenae."

The second is Alexander the Great. Consider the age at which he began his undertakings; the small means by which he carried out so dazzling a design; the authority he won, in his mere youth, with the greatest and most experienced captains in the world, who followed him; the extraordinary favour with which fortune embraced and protected so many hazardous — not to say reckless — exploits;
"Impellens quicquid sibi summa petenti Obstaret, gaudensque viam fecisse ruina;"
["Bearing down all who stood between him and the heights he sought, and pleased to force his way by ruin." — Lucan, i. 149.]

that greatness, by which at the age of thirty-three he had passed victorious through the whole habitable earth and, in half a life, reached the very limit of what human nature can achieve — so that you cannot imagine what his proper span and the continued growth of his courage and fortune would have been, had he reached due maturity of age, without imagining something more than human. Consider the many royal lines he made spring from his soldiers, leaving the world, at his death, divided among four successors — simple captains in his army — whose posterity so long held and maintained that vast inheritance. Consider so many excellent virtues he was master of: justice, temperance, generosity, truth in his word, love towards his own people, humanity towards those he overcame. His character, in general, seems incapable of any sort of reproach — though some particular and exceptional actions of his may fall under censure. But it is impossible to carry off such great things as he did within the strict rules of justice; such men are to be judged in the gross, by the main end of their actions. The destruction of Thebes and Persepolis, the murder of Menander and of Hephaestion's physician, the massacre of so many Persian prisoners at one time, of a body of Indian soldiers (not without breaking his word), and of the Cossaeans down to the children themselves, are indeed lapses not easily excused. As for Cleitus, the fault was more than redeemed; and that action, as much as any other, displays the goodness of his nature, a nature most exquisitely formed for good. It was ingeniously said of him that he had his virtues from nature and his vices from fortune. As for his being a little given to bragging, a little too impatient of hearing himself ill spoken of, and as for those mangers, weapons, and bits he had scattered about in India — all those little vanities, it seems to me, can well be allowed to his youth and to the prodigious good fortune that attended him. And anyone who will set against them his many military virtues — his diligence, foresight, patience, discipline, subtlety, magnanimity, resolution, and good luck (in which, even without Hannibal's testimony, he stood first among men) — the admirable beauty and symmetry of his person, miraculous to the point of seeming a miracle, his stately bearing and awesome look, in a face so young, ruddy, and radiant:
"Qualis, ubi Oceani perfusus Lucifer unda, Quem Venus ante alios astrorum diligit ignes, Extulit os sacrum coelo, tenebrasque resolvit;"
["As when, bathed in the waves of Ocean, Lucifer, whom Venus loves beyond the other fires of stars, lifts his sacred face to heaven and dispels the darkness." — Aeneid, iii. 589.]

the excellence of his knowledge and capacity; the length and grandeur of his glory, pure and clean, without spot or envy; the fact that long after his death it was a religious belief that even his medallions brought good fortune to those who wore them; and that more kings and princes have written about his actions than other historians have written about the actions of any other king or prince — and that even today the Mohammedans, who despise all other histories, accept and honour his alone by a special privilege: whoever, I say, will seriously consider all this will agree that, taking everything together, I had reason to set him above Caesar himself, the only one who could make me hesitate in my choice. And it cannot be denied that there was more of him in his own exploits, and more of fortune in those of Alexander. They were equal in many things, and perhaps Caesar had some greater qualities. They were two fires, two torrents, sweeping over the world by different ways:

"Ac velut immissi diversis partibus ignes Arentem in silvam, et virgulta sonantia lauro Aut ubi decursu rapido de montibus altis Dant sonitum spumosi amnes, et in aequora currunt, Quisque suum populatus iter:"

["And as fires set in different parts of a dry wood and crackling laurel shrubs, or as foaming torrents pour down from the high mountains in headlong descent and rush to the sea, each ravaging its own course." — Aeneid, xii. 521.]

but even had Caesar's ambition been more moderate, it would still be so unhappy, having the ruin of his country and the universal mischief of the world for its abominable object, that, all things put together and weighed in the balance, I must come down on Alexander's side.

The third, and in my opinion the most excellent, is Epaminondas. Of glory he has nowhere near so much as the other two (which, for that matter, is only a part of the substance of the thing); of valour and resolve — not the kind driven by ambition but the kind that wisdom and reason can plant in a well-ordered soul — he had all that could be imagined. He has, to my mind, given as ample proof of that virtue as Alexander or Caesar themselves: for although his warlike exploits were neither as frequent nor as imposing, they were, if duly weighed in all their circumstances, just as important, just as bravely fought, and carried with them as clear a testimony of valour and military skill as anyone's. The Greeks have, without dispute, done him the honour of pronouncing him the greatest man of their nation; and to be first in Greece is easily to be first in the world. As to his knowledge, we have this ancient verdict on him, "that no man ever knew so much and spoke so little as he" — for he belonged to the Pythagorean sect. But when he did speak, no one ever spoke better; an excellent orator, and a powerful persuader. But as to his character and conscience, he infinitely surpassed all men who ever undertook the conduct of affairs. For in this one thing — which ought above all to be considered, and which alone really shows what we are, and which alone, I think, outweighs all the rest put together — he comes no way short of any philosopher whatever, not even of Socrates himself. Innocence in this man is a quality peculiar, sovereign, constant, uniform, incorruptible; compared with which it appears in Alexander as subordinate, uncertain, variable, soft, and accidental.

Antiquity has judged that, if one sifts thoroughly through all the other great captains, in each one some peculiar quality stands out that gives his name lustre; but in this man alone there is a full and equal virtue throughout, leaving nothing more to wish for in him — whether in private or in public employment, whether in peace or in war, whether to live with glory and grandeur or to die. I do not know any shape or fortune of man I so much honour and love.

It is true I find his stubborn poverty, as his best friends describe it, a little too scrupulous and nice; and this is the one feature in him — high in itself, and well worthy of admiration as it is — that I find so harsh I have no wish to imitate it to the degree he carried it.

Scipio Aemilianus alone, if one could credit him with as brave and magnificent an end and as deep and universal a knowledge, might be placed in the other pan of the balance. Oh, what an injury time has done me, to deprive me of the sight of those two of the noblest lives — by the common consent of the whole world, one of the greatest of the Greeks and one of the greatest of the Romans — that were in all Plutarch. What a subject! What a workman!

For a man who was no saint but, as we say, a gentleman, of civilian and ordinary manners and of a moderate ambition, the richest life I know, and full of the richest and most desirable parts, all things considered, is in my opinion the life of Alcibiades.

But as for Epaminondas, I will add here, as an example of his exceeding goodness, some of his own opinions. He declared that the greatest satisfaction he had ever had in his whole life was the contentment he gave his father and mother by his victory at Leuctra — a great mark of deference, putting their pleasure before his own, just and full as his glory in that action was. He did not think it permissible, even to restore the liberty of his country, to kill a man without knowing the cause; which made him cold to his comrade Pelopidas' enterprise for the relief of Thebes. He was also of opinion that in battle one should avoid the encounter of a friend who was on the opposite side, and spare him. And his humanity, even towards his enemies, having made him suspect to the Boeotians — because, after he had miraculously forced the Spartans to open to him the pass they had undertaken to hold at the entry into the Morea, near Corinth, he had been content to charge through them without pursuing them to the last — they took the commission of general away from him, very honourably for him on such a ground; and to their shame they had to restore him to his command afterwards out of necessity, showing how much their safety and honour depended on him. Victory followed him like a shadow wherever he went; and indeed the prosperity of his country, being drawn from him, died with him.
